Ungrammatical 'as undisturbed as an inherited fortune' remains and 'Suppose' framing replaces the source's 'When/But if'.
replacement: When public employments are few, poorly paid, and insecure, while the various lines of business are numerous and profitable, the new and eager desires that the principle of equality produces turn from every side toward business, not toward official duties. But if, while the ranks of society are growing more equal, the education of the people stays incomplete, or their spirit is anything but bold, and if commerce and industry, held back in their growth, offer only slow and difficult ways of making a fortune, then the members of the community, despairing of improving their own condition, rush to the head of the state and demand its help. To relieve their own needs at the expense of the public treasury seems to them the easiest and most open way, if not the only one, to rise above a condition that no longer satisfies them. Place-hunting becomes the most widely followed of all trades. This must be especially so in those great centralized monarchies where paid offices are immensely numerous and the tenure of them fairly secure, so that no one despairs of getting a place and enjoying it as undisturbedly as an inherited fortune.

'perhaps be surprised' became 'may even come as a surprise', sharpening the hedge with 'even'.
replacement: Look closely at our contemporaries and dig down to the roots of their political opinions, and you will meet some of the ideas I have just described. The agreement may perhaps come as a surprise, among men who so often disagree. Americans hold that in every State the supreme power ought to come from the people. Once that power exists, however, they can imagine hardly any limit to it, and they are ready to concede that it has the right to do whatever it likes. They have not the faintest notion of special privileges for cities, families or persons. It seems never to have occurred to them that the same laws might fail to be applied, with strict uniformity, to every part and every inhabitant. These same opinions are spreading further in Europe. They are even working their way into the nations that most vehemently reject the sovereignty of the people. Those nations trace the supreme power to a different source but attribute the same characteristics to it. In all of them the idea of intermediate powers is growing faint and being erased. The idea of rights belonging inherently to certain individuals is fast vanishing from men’s minds, and the idea that society at large is omnipotent and sole authority is rising to fill the space. As social conditions grow more equal and men more alike, these ideas take root and spread. Equality produces them, and they in turn speed equality along.
